title: Who can say yes?
principle: Sell to the person who needs it, can pay, and decides.

screens.text: Let me start with a problem every seller faces. A big sale can take months of visits. If you spend those months talking to someone who cannot buy, you earn nothing. IBM, the computer company, gives its sales partners four checks to avoid this.

screens.prompt: Before spending weeks on a sale, sellers check a few things. Which one do you think they forget most?

options.label: Whether they can pay for it
Whether this person can say yes

screens.why: Many sellers forget the second one. They spend weeks talking to someone who likes them but cannot say yes. IBM's four checks cover all three things here, plus one more.

screens.title: BANT
screens.text: IBM calls its four checks BANT. Budget: can they pay? Authority: can this person say yes? Need: do they have a problem you can fix? Timing: will they buy soon? Check all four before spending more time on a buyer.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: IBM sells to big companies, but these four checks can save you time too. It's January of your fifth year at the home bakery. Each ₹850 cake leaves you ₹450. Now you want a few big buyers who order every month.

screens.prompt: An office receptionist loves your cake samples. She wants cakes for every staff birthday, but the manager signs all bills. Which check fails?
screens.why: Right. The office needs cakes, but the receptionist cannot say yes. The manager signs the bills. Ask her to help you meet the manager.

wrong.a: The problem is not about money. The receptionist likes your cakes, but the manager signs the bills. You need to meet the manager.
wrong.b: The receptionist wants cakes, so there is a need. But she cannot sign the bills. The manager decides, so you need to meet the manager.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six people who asked about your cakes. For each one, tell me: should you visit this person now?

items.text: A café owner whose snacks run out by 5 pm and who wants to start this week
A school peon who says the canteen needs cakes
A caterer who is booking cakes for parties in March
A student who wants a ₹5,000 cake but has ₹500
An office manager who signs bills and needs cakes for birthdays next week
A hotel that makes every cake in its own kitchen

screens.why: Good. The café owner, the caterer and the manager are worth visiting. The peon cannot decide, the student cannot pay, and the hotel makes its own cakes. Be kind to all six, but visit the first three.

screens.prompt: The café owner tastes a brownie and says, "Very nice! I will surely buy from you." What do you know for sure?

options.label: That he can pay your price
That he will buy this week

screens.why: Right. You learned this in Unit 2: praise is not proof. He likes your brownie, but you still need to check if he will buy. Ask for an order or a date.

wrong.b: He has not agreed to a price yet, so you do not know if he can pay. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Ask for an order or a date.
wrong.c: He has not said which day he will buy or how many brownies he wants. Remember Unit 2: praise is not proof. Ask for an order or a date.

screens.setup: It's late January. You have time for only one sales visit this week. Three people have called. Each cake leaves you ₹450.
screens.question: You can make only one visit. Who will you meet?

options.label: An IT office with 200 staff, starting in March
options.outcome: The front desk called you. You make three more visits with prices and samples. But the admin head never meets you. In March, the office chooses a chain shop. You spent four visits and ₹1,200 on samples.
options.why: The office had 200 staff, but you never met the person who could say yes. The Authority check failed. A big buyer is not useful if you cannot meet the person who decides.
options.better: Visit the factory owner. He called you himself and wants cakes from February.

options.label: A factory owner with 40 workers, starting in February
options.outcome: He called you himself, so he can decide, and he agrees to ₹850 a cake. He wants a cake for every worker's birthday from February: about 40 cakes a year. That's ₹18,000 a year for you from one visit.
options.why: He passes all four checks. He can pay, he can decide, he needs cakes, and he wants to start next month.

options.label: A chain café with 12 branches, starting next year
options.outcome: The manager likes your samples, but the café will not change bakers until next year. You spent ₹600 on samples, but you have no order yet.
options.why: The café can pay and may need you, but it will not change bakers until next year. The Timing check fails for now. Keep its number and call again when the time is closer.
options.better: Visit the factory owner. He called you himself and wants cakes from February.

screens.text: Before you spend time on a buyer, ask: can they ___, can this person ___, do they need it, and will they buy soon?
screens.why: Right. That's BANT: Budget, Authority, Need and Timing. IBM uses these checks in its sales. You can use them to sell cakes.

summary: BANT means Budget, Authority, Need and Timing. Check all four before spending time on a buyer.
Someone may like your product but may not be able to say yes. Ask to meet the person who decides.
Praise is not proof that someone will buy. Ask for an order or a date.

cards.front: A shop helper loves your product, but the owner pays all bills. Which BANT check fails?
cards.back: Authority. Ask the helper to set up a meeting with the owner.

cards.front: A café can pay, needs snacks, and the owner decides. He wants to start "sometime next year". Which check fails?
cards.back: Timing. Keep his number and call again when the date is closer.

cards.front: What do the four letters in BANT mean?
cards.back: Budget: can they pay? Authority: can they decide? Need: do they need it? Timing: will they buy soon?
